(p-212) Surah al-Ikhlas (Sincerity)

Meccan, though its status is disputed. It has four verses.

﴿Say: He is Allah, the One.﴾ The pronoun (*al-damir*) refers to the matter (*al-sha'n*), and the reason it is placed in this position, even though no antecedent has been mentioned, is to announce that the matter is so well known and prominent that everyone can call it to mind, that every pointer points to it, and that every pronoun refers back to it, as its name indicates. Its name, which is rooted in *al-qasd* (intention), is applied to the object for emphasis. Its grammatical position is the nominative as the subject (*mubtada'*), and its predicate is the sentence that follows it. No connecting pronoun is needed, because the sentence is itself the matter that the pronoun expressed. The purpose of opening the sentence with this pronoun is to draw attention, from the very beginning, to the grandeur of its content and the exalted nature of its scope, and it also adds confirmation and affirmation. A pronoun conveys at first only an ambiguous matter of great importance, so the mind remains alert for what follows that will explain it and remove its ambiguity. Thus, when the explanation arrives, it settles in the mind in the best possible way.

The hamza in *aḥad* is substituted for a *waw*, and its original form is *waḥd*. It is not like the hamza of words that are always used in negation. It is intended in a general sense, as in the Exalted's saying: ﴿So none of you could withhold Us from him.﴾ and in the saying of the Prophet, he, peace be upon him: "Spoils were not made lawful for any black-headed person other than you." In this case, the *inna* (the hamza in *aḥad*) is original. Makki said: the original form of *aḥad* is *waḥid*, and the *waw* was changed to a hamza, so two alifs came together. Since the hamza resembles the alif, one of them was deleted for ease of pronunciation. Tha'lab said: *aḥad* cannot be used as the basis for counting at the beginning, so one does not say *aḥad wa-ithnān* (one and two) as one says *wāḥid wa-ithnān*, nor does one say *rajul aḥad* (a man, one) as one says *rajul wāḥid* (one man). For this reason, it is reserved for God, the Exalted. Alternatively, the meaning is: He is exactly what you asked about, that is, the one you asked about is Allah. It has been reported that the Quraysh said: "Describe your Lord to us, the one to whom you call us, and trace His lineage," and then this was revealed. Thus the pronoun is the subject, "Allah" is its predicate, and "one" (*aḥad*) is either an apposition (*badal*) to it or a second predicate, or it is the predicate of an omitted subject.

It is also recited as "Huwa Allahu aḥad" without "qul" (say), as "Allahu aḥad" without "qul huwa," and as "Qul huwa al-Wahidu" (Say: He is the One).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 112, verse 2:

And His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Allah, the Eternal Refuge (al-Samad)﴾. It is a subject and predicate. "Al-Samad" is an intensive form (fa'al) in the sense of a passive participle (maf'ul), from samada ilayhi, meaning when one intends him (qasadahu). That is: He is the Lord (al-sayyid) to whom one turns (al-masmud ilayhi) in needs, the One who is self-sufficient in His essence, while everything other than Him is in need of Him in all its aspects. It has also been said: al-Samad is the Everlasting, the Enduring, who has never ceased and never will cease. It has also been said: He is the One who does what He wills and decides what He desires. Its definiteness (ta'rif) is because they know His samadiyyah, in contrast to His ahadiyyah (oneness). The repetition of the noble Name is to indicate that whoever does not possess this attribute is far removed from deserving divinity (uluhiyyah). The sentence is left without a conjunction (ta'riyat al-jumlah 'an al-'atif) because it is like a conclusion (natijah) to the first. He first made clear His divinity, may He be exalted and majestic, which entails all attributes of perfection; then His oneness (ahadiyyah), which requires His transcendence above any trace of plurality or composition in any respect, and any supposition of sharing in the reality or its properties; then His samadiyyah, which necessitates His essential self-sufficiency from all else and the dependence of all created things on Him for their existence, their continuance and all their conditions, as a confirmation of the truth and a guidance for them to His clear path. Then he explicitly stated some particular rulings that fall under the preceding rulings, so it is said: *

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 112, verse 3:

﴿He neither begets, nor is He begotten.﴾ This is an explicit statement refuting the claim of the slanderers concerning the angels and the Messiah. For this reason the negation is expressed in the past tense, meaning: no offspring has issued from Him, because nothing is of His kind (lit. nothing shares His genus), such that a consort of His own kind could exist for Him and they could produce offspring together, as His words, exalted is He, express: ﴿And there is not to Him any consort﴾. Nor does He need anything to assist Him or to succeed Him, since need and annihilation are impossible for Him, glorified is He. ﴿Nor is He begotten﴾, meaning: He has not issued from anything, since it is impossible to attribute non-existence to Him, either before or after. The explicit mention of this, although they acknowledge its content, serves to confirm and establish what precedes it, by indicating that the two are mutually entailed (mutually implicating, *mutalazimān*); for it is customary that whatever begets is begotten, and whatever does not beget is not begotten. Acknowledging that He is not begotten entails acknowledging that He does not beget. Thus it is close to the kind of coordination (ʿaṭf) in which the later is mentioned before the earlier, as its verification has already passed.

﴿And there is none comparable to Him.﴾ That is: no one matches Him, equals Him, or resembles Him, whether a consort or anything else. The word "لَهُ" (lahu) is a *silah* (a grammatical complement, a prepositional phrase completing the sense of the word it attaches to) of "كُفُوًا" (kufuwan). It is placed before "كُفُوًا" although its proper place is after it, for the sake of emphasis, since the intent is to negate equivalence from the Essence of God, exalted is He. It has been permitted that "لَهُ" be a *khabar* (predicate) rather than a *silah*, and that "كُفُوًا" be a *hal* (circumstantial adverbial state) of "أحَدٌ" (ahadun), but that is not the preferred view. As for the delaying of the subject of "كانَ" (kana), namely "أحَدٌ", it is for the sake of observing the *fawasil* (the rhyming final sounds of the verse endings). The connection between these sentences is clear enough that it needs no explanation.

It is also read as "كُفُؤًا" with the *kaf* and *fa* both vowelled with *damma* and the hamza eased, and as "كُفْوًا" with *kaf* vowelled with either *damma* or *kasra* and *fa* sukun.

Moreover, this noble surah, though its verses are few and close in length, contains the scattered divine knowledge and a refutation of those who deviate concerning it. It is reported in the Prophetic Hadith that it is equal to one third of the Qur'an, because the Qur'an's purposes are confined to explaining beliefs, rulings, and narratives, and whoever equates this surah with the whole of it considers its essential purpose to be that.

It is reported from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "The seven heavens and the seven earths were founded upon *Qul huwa Allahu ahad* (Say: He is God, the One)." That is: they were created only to be signs pointing to the Oneness of God and knowledge of His attributes, which this surah declares.

It is also reported from him, peace be upon him, that he heard a man reciting "قُلْ هو اللَّهُ أحَدٌ" and said: "It is due (wajabat)." It was asked: "What is due, O Messenger of God?" He said: "Paradise is due to him."
